questions.q: What makes a subquery 'correlated' rather than independent?
options: It references a column from the outer query, so it must be re-evaluated per outer row
It uses an aggregate function
It returns more than one row
It appears inside a WHERE clause
questions.explain: Independent subqueries (Lessons 52-53) have no reference to the outer query and run just once.

questions.q: How many times does a correlated subquery run?
options: Once for every row the outer query considers
Exactly once, regardless of the outer query's row count
Zero times — it's evaluated at compile time only
Twice, always
questions.explain: This re-evaluation per row is the defining characteristic of a correlated subquery.

questions.q: In the example query, why are p1 and p2 both needed, given they reference the same table?
options: Without two aliases, T-SQL couldn't distinguish the outer row's subcategory from the one being scanned inside the subquery
T-SQL requires two aliases whenever a subquery is used, regardless of correlation
p1 and p2 refer to two different physical tables
The aliases have no real purpose here and could be removed
questions.explain: This is conceptually similar to the self-join aliasing from Lesson 27, just applied inside a subquery.

questions.q: What does the correlated subquery example actually compute, compared to Lesson 52's version?
options: Products priced above average FOR THEIR OWN category, rather than above the overall average across all products
The exact same result as Lesson 52's overall average comparison
The total count of products per category
The single most expensive product in the entire table
questions.explain: The correlation to p1.ProductSubcategoryID makes the average recompute per category, not once overall.

questions.q: What is a real performance tradeoff of correlated subqueries?
options: They can be noticeably slower than an equivalent join on a large table, since they re-run per row
They are always faster than any join
They cannot be used with WHERE
They require GROUP BY to function at all
questions.explain: This performance consideration is revisited properly in the course's Performance Tuning chapter.
